===== FILE 20664__1.pdf =====
Via Regulations.gov 
 
September 3, 2025 
 
Secretary Douglas A. Collins 
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Ave. NW 
Washington, DC 20420 
 
 
RE: Reproductive Health Services, Proposed Rule, 90 F.R. 36,415 (Aug 4, 2025) (RIN 2900-
AS31) - OPPOSE 
 
Dear Secretary Collins: 
 
On behalf of more than 225,000 registered nurses across the country, including16,000 
nurses who work at 23 Veteran Health Administration facilities, National Nurses United (NNU) 
submits these comments in opposition to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) on the 
proposed rule “Reproductive Health Services” 90 F.R. 36,415 (Aug 4, 2025). As a union 
dedicated to advocating in the best interests of our patients, National Nurses United opposes 
restricting patients’ control and choices over their own health care and their own bodies. 
Restricting the right to end a pregnancy is not only bad health policy, it violates the nursing 
ethics NNU members pledge to uphold. Nurses have a duty to advocate for our patients and their 
right to make their own health care decisions. The basic tenets of ethical health care dictate that 
patients should enjoy autonomy, self-determination, and dignity over their bodies, their lives, and 
the health care they receive. Forcing a patient to give birth against their will violates those tenets. 
For these reasons and the reasons discussed below, National Nurses United strongly and 
unequivocally urges you to withdraw the proposed rule and to preserve and expand access 
to abortion services and counseling through the VA and the Civilian Health and Medical 
Program of the VA. 
 
I. Reproductive rights are human rights. 
This anti-abortion proposed rule is part of the administration’s systematic campaign to 
undo hard-won human and civil rights in the United States, and to control working people by 
removing their power and bodily autonomy. This rule goes against the beliefs and values of the 
vast majority of people in the United States and is an attack on democracy itself.  
 
Reproductive justice is requisite for any democracy where working people truly have a 
say in our workplaces and communities. Restrictions on abortion, like all other restrictions on 
access to health care, prevent people from participating in our democracy and economy. 
Abortion access also allows women to focus on education, training and/or working which leads 
to greater economic security and opportunity to more fully participate in democracy. For women 
to have a voice at work, provide for our families, and advocate for ourselves politically, we must 
have the right to maintain bodily autonomy, including when and whether to have children.  
 

National Nurses United Comments  
re: “Reproductive Health Services,” Proposed Rule, 90 F.R. 36,415 (Aug 4, 2025) 
RIN 2900-AS31 
September 3, 2025 
Page 2 
Nurses know that abortion bans do not stop abortions but make them more expensive and 
harder to access. This denial of health care will most harm and deepen existing inequalities for 
low-income veterans, and veterans who already suffer from lack of adequate health care, such as 
Black, Latinx, and immigrant women. 
 
II. Abortion is a needed medical service. 
The VA has been tasked by Congress to provide “needed” hospital care and medical 
services to veterans.1 In the proposed rule, the VA claims that abortion care is not “needed.” This 
is false. As health care professionals and members of a profession that is 90 percent female, 
nurses know that abortion care is necessary medical care.  
 
Without access to abortion services, patients may be at risk of illness and death due to 
pregnancy. From a medical perspective, pregnancy is far more dangerous than abortion.2 One 
study comparing the mortality risk of induced abortion to the mortality risk of staying pregnant 
found that “in 2020, staying pregnant was 35–39 times deadlier than induced abortion.”3 
Pregnancy also causes severe maternal morbidity—significant short-term or long-term 
consequences to a woman’s health as an outcome of labor and delivery—at a rate of 70 cases per 
every pregnancy-related death.4 The risk of morbidity would be ignored under the proposed rule. 
 
Few of the services in the medical benefits package have the potential impact on 
mortality and morbidity as abortion care. The medical benefits package appropriately includes 
services like bereavement counseling, reconstructive plastic surgery required as a result of 
trauma, prosthetics, and a wide range of outpatient medical care and prescription drugs. These 
services are recognized as needed health care and they have a huge impact on the quality of life 
of our patients, but in many cases the life of the patient would not be at risk without them. 
Restricting abortion to cases of life endangerment but not health endangerment is inconsistent 
with the definition of “needed” used in the rest of the list. This difference is based in a hostility 
to reproductive rights that amounts to discrimination against women veterans and Civilian Health 
and Medical Program enrollees.  
 
As explained in the 2022 rulemaking, the choice of some states to criminalize abortion 
care unfairly deprives veterans in those states of access to abortion, making their ability to access 
this care at the VA in those states critically important. Veterans and their family members should 
have the right to seek abortion care from their trusted VA health care providers. 
 
III. Abortion bans kill women despite having “life of the mother” exceptions on paper. 
The proposed rule would exclude abortion from VA medical services “except when a 
physician certifies that the life of the mother would be endangered if the fetus were carried to 
 
1 38 U.S. Code § 1710. 
2 Adebayo Adesomo. “Pregnancy Is Far More Dangerous Than Abortion.” May 30, 2022. Scientific American. 
https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/pregnancy-is-far-more-dangerous-to-women-than-abortion/.  
3 AJ Stevenson, E Raymond, D Grossman. “Comparing Mortality Risk of Induced Abortion with Mortality Risk of 
Staying Pregnant.” Contraception. Volume 127, 110150, November 2023. 
4 Roy Ahn, at al. “Initiatives to Reduce Maternal Mortality and Severe Maternal Morbidity in the United States: A 
Narrative Review.” Ann Intern Med.2020;173:S3-S10. doi:10.7326/M19-3258. 

National Nurses United Comments  
re: “Reproductive Health Services,” Proposed Rule, 90 F.R. 36,415 (Aug 4, 2025) 
RIN 2900-AS31 
September 3, 2025 
Page 3 
term.” This is a shockingly restrictive ban that will not protect pregnant veterans and others 
affected by this rule. 
 
“Life of the mother” exceptions do not protect patients’ lives or health. Over the years 
since the Supreme Court permitted states to take away their residents’ right to abortion in Dobbs 
v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, 142 S. Ct. 2228 (2022), we have seen a series of 
horrifying medical crises inflicted on patients due to state abortion bans. Women have gone to 
emergency rooms in these states suffering serious medical crises due to miscarriages and been 
turned away.5 Some women have died preventable deaths due to delays in needed care caused by 
abortion bans.6 After Texas banned abortion in 2021, the rates of sepsis and blood transfusions 
associated with pregnancy loss rose by 50% and 54%.7 Doctors and hospital legal departments 
are afraid to provide life-saving care because they fear prosecution by authorities second-
guessing their medical opinions. Health care professionals should not have to put our licenses, 
jobs, and freedom at risk to provide the care that our patients need.  
 
IV. Conclusion 
The ban proposed in this rule is one of the strictest in the country.8 The existing rule 
already provides extremely limited abortion access. This rule would go further by taking away 
exceptions for the health of the patient and for rape or incest. This is an extreme limitation on 
safety and bodily autonomy. Abortion access should be expanded beyond the limited 
circumstances allowed under the existing rule, not further restricted. Thus, we urge you to 
withdraw this rule endangering the health of veterans and their families and blocking us 
from providing care that our veterans and their families need. 
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Michelle Grisat 
National Director of Health and Regulatory Policy 
National Nurses United
